query: microVM Firecracker pool orchestration multi-tenant AI agent sandbox autoscaling 2026
read:
Kata Containers orchestrates multiple VMMs (Firecracker, Cloud Hypervisor, QEMU) to provide microVM isolation through standard container APIs.

It integrates with Kubernetes, handling all operational complexity of running microVMs. From Kubernetes' perspective, it's a normal container. Under the hood, it's a full VM with hardware isolation.

Security model: Same hardware-level isolation as Firecracker, with Kubernetes-native orchestration.

Performance: Boots in ~200ms, minimal memory overhead.

Use case: Production Kubernetes workloads needing VM-level security with container workflows.
snippet:
Firecracker creates lightweight virtual machines with minimal device emulation, running each microVM with its own Linux kernel inside KVM.

Security model: Hardware-level isolation. Each workload has a dedicated kernel completely separated from the host. Attackers must escape both the guest kernel and the hypervisor.

Performance: Boots in ~125ms, less than 5 MiB overhead per VM, up to 150 VMs per second per host.

claim: This is a concrete, dated (GA June 2026) named allocation model for fleets of short-lived agent sandboxes: no shared pool, one Firecracker microVM per tenant, with a three-state lifecycle (active / suspended-snapshot / reaped) run by an orchestrator plus a sweeper. Cold start is expensive only once per tenant (~90s first turn) because later turns resume a memory snapshot in seconds; a fully idle tenant costs near-$0 because it is reaped and only its state persists on EFS. 8-hour hard lifetime caps how long any one microVM runs.
query: microVM Firecracker pool orchestration multi-tenant AI agent sandbox autoscaling 2026
read: One isolated Firecracker MicroVM per tenant — cold-started, resumed, and reaped on demand. An idle tenant's VM auto-suspends; a fully idle tenant is terminated and its state parks on EFS for =$0. The platform suspends/resumes on traffic; the orchestrator cold-starts dead tenants on demand and a sweeper reaps idle ones. Resuming a suspended MicroVM restores the Firecracker snapshot -- process memory and all -- in ~seconds. The first turn cold-starts the tenant's MicroVM (~90s); later turns are warm. Built on AWS Lambda MicroVMs (GA June 2026). Firecracker-isolated, snapshot-resumable serverless compute with an 8-hour lifetime.
snippet: Multi-tenant AI agents on AWS Lambda MicroVMs — one Firecracker VM per tenant with near-zero idle cost, snapshot resume, auto lifecycle, and EFS-persisted state.

claim: Three distinct GPU-sharing mechanisms exist for fleets of concurrent workloads, trading isolation for density: time-slicing (software-only, any NVIDIA GPU, up to 48 concurrent, zero memory isolation), MIG (hardware-partitioned, compute capability >=8.0 only, up to 7 isolated instances per H100), and MPS (concurrent kernel execution, up to 60 concurrent, limited fault protection). Published 2026-09-08, inside the recency window. Real production GPU utilization is reported as low as 5% average without active bin-packing, which is the gap fractional sharing and schedulers are sold against.
query: GPU MIG time-slicing fractional allocation Kubernetes AI agents 2026
read: Time-Slicing: allows multiple workloads to share a single physical GPU by rapidly switching between processes; works on any NVIDIA GPU; up to 48 concurrent workloads per GPU; no memory isolation -- GPU memory is shared between all processes. MIG (Multi-Instance GPU): partitions the physical GPU into isolated slices at the silicon level; requires compute capability >= 8.0 (A100, A30, H100, H200, B200, GB200); a single H100 80GB supports up to 7 MIG instances using the 1g.10gb profile; each slice gets dedicated memory, cache, and Streaming Multiprocessors. MPS (Multi-Process Service): enables truly concurrent kernel execution from different processes; each client has an isolated address space, but fault protection is limited; supports up to 60 concurrent workloads on Volta+ GPUs. Average GPU utilization in production Kubernetes clusters is just 5%; the best-performing cluster achieved 49% utilization, roughly 10x the average; teams using Cast AI automation moved utilization to the 40-60% range. DRA (Dynamic Resource Allocation) on Kubernetes 1.34+: time-slicing configurable via a shared ResourceClaim with timeSlicingConfig intervals; MIG assignment through a ResourceClaimTemplate with device profile selectors; MPS configured with CUDA_MPS_ACTIVE_THREAD_PERCENTAGE and memory limits.
snippet: Average GPU utilization in production Kubernetes clusters is just 5%, according to the Cast AI 2026 State of Kubernetes Optimization Report.
title: Fractional GPUs in Kubernetes: Right-Size AI Workloads

claim: Kubernetes DRA (ResourceClaim/ResourceClaimTemplate/DeviceClass, with CEL-based device-attribute filtering) is the closest thing found to an open schema for declaring a compute/device resource request richer than the OCI Runtime Spec's cgroup-style CPU/memory limits -- it lets a workload claim a device (e.g. a GPU, or a fraction/MIG slice of one) by class and attribute rather than by bare quantity. It is not a cross-runtime OCI-level standard the way the Runtime Spec is: it is a Kubernetes API, first available in v1.30, stable since v1.35 per this page, governed under kubernetes-sigs (CNCF-adjacent, in-project). A separate search result (search-only, not fetched) described it as having 'graduated to GA in Kubernetes 1.34' -- the two sources disagree on the exact stabilization release; recorded as-seen rather than reconciled.
query: open standard schema declaring compute resource request beyond OCI runtime spec Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation 2026
read: With DRA, device drivers and cluster admins define device classes that are available to claim in workloads. Kubernetes allocates matching devices to specific claims and places the corresponding Pods on nodes that can access the allocated devices. With DRA, app operators don't need to specify device quantities in Pod resource requests; instead, the Pod references a resource claim, and the device configuration in that claim applies to the Pod. You can share the same resource with multiple containers or Pods by referencing the corresponding resource claim. Create ResourceClaims or ResourceClaimTemplates to request specific configurations within DeviceClasses, using common expression language (CEL) to perform fine-grained filtering for specific device attributes. Feature state: Stable since Kubernetes v1.35. This is a stable feature in Kubernetes, and has been since version v1.35. It was first available in the v1.30 release.
snippet: DRA is a Kubernetes feature that lets you request and share resources among Pods. These resources are often attached devices like hardware accelerators.

claim: An agent that only calls a hosted model API (Anthropic, OpenAI, etc.) needs no GPU of its own -- the provider abstracts all hardware, quota, and provisioning concerns away from the caller. GPU pooling and fractional-allocation questions (MIG/time-slicing/MPS, DRA) apply specifically to the self-hosted-inference path, matching this repo's own REF-8-02 framing of inference as swappable between 'a local serving engine on owned GPUs' and 'any OpenAI-compatible server.' query: does agent need GPU hosted model API vs self-hosted inference compute
read: Hardware Management: Abstracted away [for serverless] / Requires GPU setup & maintenance [for self-hosted]. Self-hosting LLMs at scale usually requires high-end GPUs (such as NVIDIA A100 or H100); serverless APIs abstract these hardware complexities. Self-hosting can achieve up to 6x lower cost than serverless APIs at sufficient scale.

claim: Run:ai is a named fleet-level GPU pooling/scheduling system: it tracks a guaranteed per-project quota (deservedGpus, never preempted) plus a weighted over-quota borrowing scheme (overQuotaWeight) so idle GPU capacity across many tenants is redistributed proportionally rather than sitting idle, and uses gang scheduling to place multi-node jobs atomically only once every required GPU is free. Document uses GPU pricing dated 2026-05-13, inside the recency window.
query: GPU MIG time-slicing fractional allocation Kubernetes AI agents 2026
read: Memory is not partitioned; both workloads share the same GPU memory address space without enforcement of per-workload limits. deservedGpus is the allocation that Run:ai will never preempt. overQuotaWeight determines how idle capacity is distributed -- a project with weight 3 gets three times as much over-quota capacity as a project with weight 1 when both are competing for free GPUs. Worked example: a 16-GPU cluster with three teams at 8/4/2 deserved GPUs yields over-quota shares of 60%/20%/20% when all compete simultaneously. Run:ai's gang scheduling holds all pod placement decisions for a job until GPUs are available on all required nodes simultaneously, then places them atomically. If Run:ai's fractional scheduling and over-quota borrowing recover 20% GPU utilization on a 16-GPU cluster, that recovers 3.2 GPU-years of capacity.
snippet: A workload requesting 0.5 GPU gets scheduled on a physical GPU alongside another 0.5 GPU workload. The GPU executes their kernels in alternating time slices.

claim: Modal exposes three explicit autoscaling knobs for bursty, short-lived agent-style workloads on top of a roughly 1-second base container boot: buffer_containers (provision ahead of predicted burst), min_containers (a warm floor so the function never fully scales to zero), and scaledown_window (idle time before scale-to-zero, default 60s, configurable up to 20 minutes). This is a concrete, named alternative pattern to the per-tenant microVM model in X-refmodel-4-2-compute-002: a shared function-level container pool with tunable warm/idle policy rather than one long-lived VM per tenant.
query: Modal.com container pool warm pool scale to zero cold start milliseconds 2026
read: Containers boot in about one second. buffer_containers provisions extra containers while the Function is active, particularly useful for bursty request patterns, where the arrival of one input predicts the arrival of more inputs. min_containers establishes a baseline to prevent functions from scaling entirely to zero during idle periods. By default, the maximum idle time is 60 seconds, which can be extended up to twenty minutes via the scaledown_window parameter. For models in the tens of gigabytes, pre-downloading rather than fetching during initialization can reduce boot times from minutes to seconds.
snippet: Containers boot in about one second.

claim: Checkpoint/restore of a process's full memory state (not just container image caching) is the concrete mechanism cutting a torch-import cold start from ~5s to ~1.05s p50 (2.5x) by replacing ~26,000 filesystem syscalls with one memory-mapped file load -- the same class of technique as Firecracker/E2B snapshot-restore (X-unit-design-003, ~150ms) but measured on a heavier ML-import workload. Modal's own implementation is explicitly reactive (snapshot taken and reused on demand) rather than a proactively pre-warmed pool, a design choice worth contrasting with warm-pool approaches when this card is written up.
query: Modal.com container pool warm pool scale to zero cold start milliseconds 2026
read: Memory snapshot restore is about 2.5x faster than a standard container startup. A simple `import torch` example program takes normally around 5 seconds to cold start; with snapshot restore it's around 1.05 seconds at p50. Python's import system is filesystem-based and needs to execute thousands of slow, sequential filesystem operations -- importing torch alone executes 26,000 syscalls. Checkpoint/restore turns thousands of syscalls into (roughly) a single file load, recreating the process's memory mappings directly. Snapshots are created on-demand when Modal's scheduler finds that it does not have an existing active Function snapshot available -- i.e. reactively, not as a pre-warmed pool.
snippet: A Modal memory snapshot is a couple of files that represent the entire state of a Linux container right before it was about to accept a request.
title: Memory snapshots: Checkpoint/restore for sub-second startup
topic: Checkpoint/restore memory snapshots as the mechanism behind sub-second warm starts
